intro: WELCOME. This is a realistic-opponent repertoire for BLACK built around the Caro-Kann Defence — the most solid and reliable answer to 1.e4 there is. Black plays 1...c6 and 2...d5, accepts a locked pawn chain, develops the light-squared bishop to f5 BEFORE playing ...e6, and then outplays White in a sound, healthy middlegame. It is a fighting but low-risk opening: the structures are easy to remember and Black is almost never mated in the opening. Built the same way as the companion King's Indian, Sicilian, Queen's Gambit, Indian Defenses, English Opening, King's Indian Attack, London System and Colle System encyclopedias: main plans, the tries you'll actually meet, sharp lines, typical mistakes, every line verified move-by-move for legality. Chapter 1: Understanding the Caro-Kann (why ...c6 first, the ...d5 break, the f5 bishop, the locked chain, and the two pawn structures you must recognise). Chapter 2: The Classical Variation (3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5). Chapter 3: The Advance Variation (3.e5). Chapter 4: The Exchange Variation and the Panov-Botvinnik Attack (3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 / 4.c4). Chapter 5: The Two Knights (4...Nd7) and the Fantasy (3.f3). Chapter 6: Black's Plans in the Middlegame. Chapter 7: Traps and Tactics. Every line is completed to fifteen moves for each side with engine-verified top play, and every coach comment is preserved.

studies.title: Study 1.1 — Why the Caro-Kann? The ...c6/...d5 Idea

tree.commentAfter: White takes the centre. The Caro-Kann is one of the most reliable answers there is: Black builds a rock-solid structure and takes the fight to White later.

THE DEFINING MOVE, AND IT COMES FIRST. ...c6 prepares ...d5 while keeping the c8-bishop's diagonal open. Compare 1...e6 (the French): same idea, but there the bishop is already shut in. The move order is the whole opening.
White takes the full centre. Good — this is the position Black wants to see.
The point of ...c6. Black challenges e4 at once and accepts a locked chain in return for a sound, tension-free structure.

variations.commentAfter: White chooses the ADVANCE instead of 3.Nc3. The pawn goes to e5 and the structure changes character completely: White gains space but gives up the tension, and the c8-bishop's diagonal is now permanently open.
THE ONLY GOOD ANSWER. Black must attack the head of the chain immediately. Passively defending lets White build up with Nf3, Be2, O-O and then push f4.
White supports d4 and prepares to meet ...cxd4 with cxd4, keeping the chain intact.
Black increases the pressure on d4. Notice how the whole plan is already visible: ...Qb6, ...Nh6 or ...Bg6, and the d4-pawn is the target.
White defends d4 with the knight and keeps developing.

THE POINT OF THE CARO-KANN MOVE ORDER AGAIN. The bishop develops OUTSIDE the chain, pinning the f3-knight. Had Black played ...e6 first, this bishop would be stuck behind its own pawns — which is exactly the French Defence's problem.
White breaks the pin and prepares to castle. The bishop on e2 is modest but safe.
Black completes the chain. Now both sides have a fixed structure and the game becomes a question of which attack arrives first — White's f4-f5 or Black's ...cxd4 and ...Nge7-f5.

tree.commentAfter: White defends e4 and develops. 3.e5 is the Advance (Ch 3) and 3.exd5 the Exchange (Ch 4); 3.Nc3 invites the Classical.
Black clarifies the centre. The e4-pawn had to be addressed, and this is the Classical choice — it opens lines for the c8-bishop, which is exactly why Black played ...c6 before ...e6.
White recaptures, and the knight is now a target. Notice that Black has not committed a single pawn beyond the third rank.
THE CLASSICAL BISHOP SORTIE. This is the move the whole move order was designed for: the problem bishop reaches its best diagonal BEFORE ...e6 can bury it behind the pawn chain.
White kicks the bishop; this is the main line of the Classical.
The bishop retreats to g6, where it is safe, still eyes e4, and cannot be attacked by a pawn.
White grabs space and threatens h5, hitting the bishop. This is the critical try.

variations.commentAfter: The solid alternative to ...h6: Black prepares ...Nf6 and ...c5 without committing the h-pawn. Less forcing, but very hard to break, and it keeps the option of ...h5 in some positions.
White develops and keeps the tension in the centre.
Black completes queenside development and prepares both ...Ngf6 and ...c5.
White offers the bishop trade.
Black takes — the same logic as the main line.
White recaptures.
Black develops, and will follow with ...Be7 and ...O-O. This is the Caro-Kann at its most comfortable: no weaknesses, no targets, and a clear plan.
Book line ends here — engine-verified top play completes the line to 15 moves for each side.

tree.commentAfter: Black makes room for the bishop on h7 — the standard reply and the tabiya of the Classical Caro-Kann. Everything from here is a middlegame fight.
White develops and prepares to castle.
Black develops the queen's knight, keeping ...Ngf6 in reserve and preparing ...c5. The knight on d7 also supports a later ...e5 break.
White commits the pawn and forces the bishop to h7, where it is a little passive — but it is still safe, and White has spent a tempo.
The bishop goes to h7. It looks cramped, and it is — but it is also unattackable, and it still watches the g6 and e4 squares.
White offers the trade of the good bishops.
Black accepts. Trading is right here: the bishop on h7 is the least active piece Black owns, and removing it costs nothing.
White recaptures with the queen, which is slightly awkward — the queen is not ideally placed on d3, and it will be a target for ...c5 and ...Nb6.
NOW ...e6 is correct. With the bishop already developed and traded, the pawn move only supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop. This is the whole lesson of the move order.
White develops the bishop and prepares to castle queenside.
Black completes development. Both sides are castling on opposite wings, which means a race — and Black's is the easier one to conduct.
White castles long. The pawns in front of the king are untouched, but so is the file the rooks will open.
Black castles next move and then plays on the queenside with ...c5 and ...b5. A fully equal, healthy position — which is the honest promise of the Caro-Kann.

studies.title: Study 1.2 — The Locked Chain: Reading the Advance Structure

tree.commentAfter: The second structure you must recognise. White pushes past the tension instead of trading, and the whole game takes on a French-like character — except that Black's bishop is OUTSIDE the chain.
The Caro-Kann.
White builds the big centre.
Black challenges it.
THE ADVANCE. White closes the centre rather than trade. The pawn on e5 gains space and fixes the structure, but it also gives Black a clear target and a clear plan.

The key difference from the French. Black's bishop comes out to f5 FIRST, where it is active and outside the pawn chain. In the French this piece would be buried on c8 for the whole game — that single difference is why the Caro-Kann is considered the safer French.

variations.commentAfter: White develops the bishop BEFORE playing Nf3 — a different move order with a concrete point: the bishop may be traded for Black's good bishop on f5.
Black takes. The alternative is to retreat, but that concedes the diagonal and gives White a free tempo, so the trade is the honest choice.
White recaptures with the queen, which is slightly awkward — the queen on d3 can be hit by ...c5 with tempo in some lines.
Black builds the chain. The structure is now the classic Advance Caro-Kann: White's pawn on e5 against Black's pawns on e6 and d5.
White finally develops the knight, defending d4 and preparing to castle.
Black strikes at the base of the chain. This is the move the whole setup is built around — without it, Black has no counterplay at all.
White holds the centre together. The tension on d4 is now permanent.
Black adds a third attacker to d4. The position is balanced: White has space, Black has a target and no weaknesses.

tree.commentAfter: White develops and prepares to support d4 and the kingside.
Now Black supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop. The chain is fixed: White's pawns on d4/e5 against Black's on d5/e6.
White develops and prepares to castle.
THE BREAK. Black attacks the base of White's chain. Every plan in this structure starts with this move — it is the Caro-Kann's answer to a space disadvantage.
White defends d4 and offers the trade of dark-squared bishops.

variations.commentAfter: The immediate release, without ...Nc6 first. Also perfectly playable and slightly more forcing — but Black keeps the knight on b8, which makes ...b5 and ...Nc6 a later option.
White recaptures.
Black develops the knight to e7, NOT f6 — with White's pawn on e5, ...Nf6 simply drops the knight to exf6. The knight heads for f5 instead, where it attacks d4 and e3.
White defends.

Black develops the OTHER knight. Note that Be7 is impossible here: the knight is sitting on e7, so the f8-bishop has no square to go to and Black simply develops the queenside knight instead. The structure is the same as the main line, reached a move earlier.

tree.commentAfter: Black adds a third attacker to d4 and develops. Now the pressure on White's centre is real.
White defends d4 a third time. The tension is at its peak, and Black must decide when to release it.
The release. Trading on d4 leaves White with an isolated pawn after the recapture — a permanent structural weakness and a permanent target.
White recaptures with the knight, keeping the pawn structure intact.
Black takes the knight. Removing a defender of d4 and simplifying towards a position where the isolated pawn is a pure liability.
White recaptures with the bishop — the recapture Black wanted. White's d-pawn is now isolated, and the whole middlegame plan for Black writes itself: blockade d4, trade pieces, and win the endgame.

THE CORRECT DEVELOPMENT. The knight comes to e7, heading for f5 — and note what Black does NOT play here: ...Nf6 would lose the knight to exf6, because White's pawn is still standing on e5. ...Qb6 is even worse: White's bishop on d4 attacks b6 through the empty c5 square, so Bxb6 wins the queen for a bishop. This is exactly the move-order trap the SEE gate missed and a hand trace caught — the queen belongs on b6 only BEFORE the d4 exchanges.
White castles. Black has achieved the ideal outcome of the Advance: no weaknesses of his own, and a target that will not move.

studies.title: Study 2.1 — The Classical Main Line: 6.h4 h6

tree.commentAfter: The Classical is the main road of the Caro-Kann and the one you will meet most often against a prepared opponent.
The Caro-Kann.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
The Classical move order. White defends e4 and develops at the same time.
Black releases the tension, opening the c8-bishop's diagonal.
White recaptures. The knight on e4 is the key piece of the whole variation — and the key target.
The bishop comes out. Black is threatening ...Bxe4 followed by ...Qxd4 in some lines, so White must be careful.
The main move: White kicks the bishop and keeps the knight on the board. 5.Ng3 is why this is called the Classical.
The bishop retreats. It keeps an eye on e4 and cannot be attacked again by a pawn.

variations.commentAfter: White declines to play h4. This is the quieter treatment: White develops normally and lets Black commit first.
Black takes the opportunity to support d5 and free the f8-bishop. There is no need for ...h6 now, because h4 is not coming.
White offers the trade.

White DECLINES the h4-h5 pawn storm and develops quietly. This is the positional approach: no commitment, no weaknesses, and the option of h4 later once the pieces are placed.
Black develops the knight — the natural route is now open, because White has not driven the bishop away or grabbed h5.
White captures the e4-pawn, opening the position. This is the trade that defines the line: the knight on e4 must be met accurately.

Black recaptures with the BISHOP, not the knight. This is the accurate move: the bishop was doing nothing on g6 (its diagonal is blocked), and recapturing with it both centralises it and keeps the d7-knight free to go to f6 without blocking the f8-bishop.
White offers the trade of the good bishop.
Black accepts. Exchanging is right here: leaving the bishop on e4 after Qxd3 would let White play Bxe4 at a moment of their choosing, and the bishop on d3 is the piece that eyes h7.
White recaptures, and the queen on d3 is well placed, eyeing the queenside.
Black completes the chain, prepares ...Be7 and ...O-O, and reaches a sound, slightly passive position that is very hard to break down.

tree.commentAfter: The critical try. White wants h5 to drive the bishop to h7 and gain space on the kingside.

THE STANDARD REPLY. Black gives the bishop a bolt-hole on h7. This position — pawns on h4/h6, bishop on g6 — is the tabiya of the Classical Caro-Kann and the single most important position in this repertoire.
White completes development and prepares Bd3 to offer the trade.
Black develops and prepares ...Ngf6, ...c5 and possibly ...e5. The knight on d7 is more flexible than on c6 here.
White forces the issue. The pawn advances and attacks the bishop, which must go to h7.
The bishop retreats to h7. It looks passive and it is — but it is completely safe there, and White has spent two tempi and weakened g5 and h5 to achieve nothing concrete.
White offers the trade of the light-squared bishops.
Black accepts. Always trade this bishop if White offers it: it is Black's least active piece, and its departure removes any chance of it becoming a target.
White recaptures with the queen. The queen is now on a slightly exposed square and will be hit by ...c5 and ...Nb6 later.
Only now. The bishop is already gone, so ...e6 simply supports d5 and frees the f8-bishop. This is the Caro-Kann's move order working exactly as designed.
White develops and prepares to castle queenside.
THE TACTICAL POINT. With White's bishop committed to f4, the queen check forces the bishop back to d2 — gaining a tempo and clearing the way for ...Qc7 and long castling.
White blocks. Forced: 12.Nd2?? would lose the knight to ...Qxd2+.
The queen retreats to its best square, eyeing h2 and preparing ...O-O-O.
White castles long. Both kings are now on opposite wings, and the game becomes a race.
Black completes development and prepares ...O-O. The position is balanced, but Black's play is much easier to conduct: the pawn structure is sound and every piece has a clear square.

THE OTHER STANDARD REPLY — and it is a real choice, not a formality. By playing ...h5 Black blocks the pawn on h4 permanently and removes the h5 threat, at the cost of fixing the kingside structure and giving White a target on g7.
White develops and prepares to castle. The h4-pawn is now blocked and will stay there for the rest of the game — a dead pawn rather than a battering ram.
Black develops the queen's knight, keeping ...Ngf6 in reserve and preparing ...c5.
White completes the kingside setup. Note 5.Bd3 is not yet available as a trade offer: the bishop on f5 has not committed to g6, so White develops modestly and keeps the option of Nf5 in reserve.
Black develops the last minor piece, covering e4 and preparing to castle.
NOW White offers the trade, once the black bishop has committed to g6.

Black drops the bishop back, still outside the chain and still eyeing e4. The blocked h-pawns mean Black's king is safe and the game is a slow manoeuvring fight — exactly the character of this variation.

White offers the trade.
Black accepts — always trade this bishop when offered.

Supporting d5 and freeing the f8-bishop. Note that Black still has not played ...h6, because there is no pawn coming to h4.

Black completes kingside development.
White strikes in the centre. This is the standard plan against Black's setup: open lines while the pieces are still being placed.
Black develops calmly and prepares to castle. There is no need to fear cxd5 — Black recaptures with the knight or the pawn and stays solid.
White prepares Bb2 to fight for the long diagonal.
Black castles. The king is safe and the rooks are connected.
White completes the fianchetto, aiming the bishop at g7.
THE BREAK, and the thematic move of the whole repertoire. Black strikes at the base of White's centre, and the resulting trades leave Black with the better pawn structure.

The Advance is the most popular try against the Caro-Kann at club level, because it looks like it refutes the opening by gaining space. It does not — but you must know the plan.
The Caro-Kann.
White takes the centre.
Black challenges it.
THE ADVANCE. White declines the trade and closes the centre. The pawn on e5 gains space and fixes the structure — but it also gives Black a clear target and a clear plan.
The bishop comes out FIRST, before ...e6. This is the move that makes the Caro-Kann better than the French against the Advance: the bishop is outside the chain and active.

variations.commentAfter: White develops the knight BEFORE Nf3 — the main-line move order against the Advance. The knight on c3 supports the e4-square and prepares the f4 break, but it also blocks the c-pawn and the queen's route to c2.
Black starts the chain. The bishop is already out on f5, which is the whole point of ...Bf5 before ...e6 in the Advance.
White completes the kingside development and prepares Be2 and O-O.
Black develops the queen's knight. From d7 it supports ...c5, the move the whole structure demands, and it does not block the f8-bishop.
White completes the kingside setup, preparing to castle short.
The bishop retreats to g6. It is safe there, still eyes e4, and — crucially — it is now OUTSIDE the pawn chain, which is the difference between this and the French Defence.
White castles. The kingside pawns stay on f2, g2 and h2 for now, ready to advance.
THE MOVE THAT GIVES THE STRUCTURE ITS MEANING. Black must chip at d4 or the position plays itself for White, who will eventually roll forward with f4-f5.

White develops and prepares to castle.
THE FLEXIBLE SETUP. Black develops the queen's knight to d7 instead of c6, keeping ...c5 in reserve and preparing ...Ne7 and ...Nf5 or ...c5 depending on what White does.
White castles short.
The bishop retreats to g6, where it is safe and still watches e4 and f5. Note that Black has not yet committed ...c5 — that is the whole point of ...Nd7.
White prepares to defend d4 with b4 or to play Be3.
Black reroutes the knight to f5, where it will attack d4 and e3. This is the classic Advance plan: Black's pieces converge on the base of White's chain.
White develops and defends d4 a third time.

variations.commentAfter: Another good plan: Black puts the queen on c7 first, supporting ...c5 and ...b5 and keeping the centre flexible.
White defends e5 and prepares Nf1-g3.
Now the break comes, with the queen behind it.
White takes, releasing the tension.
Black recaptures with the knight from d7. The position is balanced, and Black has a comfortable game with the bishop on g6 and a clear plan on the queenside.

The Advance.

Black builds the chain, comfortable in the knowledge that White has not yet committed a single pawn beyond the third rank on the kingside.
White develops and defends d4.

The Advance.

THE IMMEDIATE BREAK. Black attacks d4 before completing development. The point: White's centre is over-extended, and every trade on d4 improves Black's structure.

variations.commentAfter: White builds the standard setup rather than attacking the bishop immediately with Nc3 or c4. The queen on d3 defends the e4-pawn, connects with the bishop on e2, and keeps the f1-rook free to come to d1.

THE ACTIVE SQUARE. The queen offers a trade and puts pressure on d4 at the same time. Trading queens would suit Black perfectly — it removes White's attacking chances and leaves a comfortable endgame.
White develops the knight and declines the queen trade by simply not offering it. The position is a strategic tug-of-war with no forced tactics.
Black develops, adding a defender to d4 and preparing ...Nge7 or ...Nge7-f5.
White takes on c5, resolving the central tension while the queen on b6 is loose.
